headline: I Am Thrilled To Finally Stop Attaching My Voter Form To A Hand-Drawn Map Of My Great-Grandfather’s Cattle Shed
body:
For the past three election cycles, I have spent upwards of six weeks documenting the precise geographical coordinates of my ancestral grain storage unit just to qualify for a ballot. The Election Commission’s previous requirement for an 'Added Declaration' meant that if I couldn't provide a notarized sketch of where my family kept their pulses in 1948, my application was returned with a red stamp that simply read: 'INSUFFICIENT RURAL NOSTALGIA.'

I had become quite the amateur cartographer, spending my weekends measuring the distance between the old pump and the village banyan tree. I kept a ledger of the specific dimensions of every dry-waste pit on our ancestral property, fearing that a single missing centimeter would disenfranchise me. It felt like I was applying for a zoning permit for an imaginary civilization rather than just trying to vote for the local councilor.

Now, with the commission dropping that specific declaration for my state, I find myself in a strange sort of existential void. I have all these detailed blueprints and architectural diagrams of my family's historic poultry coops, and no bureaucrat to judge them. I suppose I’ll have to go back to just voting based on party manifestos, but honestly, it’s going to be hard to get the same rush of adrenaline I got from successfully documenting a structural survey of a shed built during the British Raj.
caption: Goodbye to the days of drawing maps to prove I exist. My desk is finally free of protractors and ancestral livestock charts. Democracy is getting easier, but my interior design skills are suffering. #VoterID #Bureaucracy #ElectionCommission (satire)
igHook: Ever had to submit a blood oath just to get your voter card processed?
imagePrompt: A cluttered wooden desk covered in various hand-drawn, sepia-toned sketches of rural farm structures, grain silos, and measurement tapes, with a pair of reading glasses resting on top of a stack of government forms.
